content.thinking:
I need to be careful not to restate the given cost figures as if I computed them, and not invent my own numbers. For duration, I should stick to what's known as a lower bound rather than fabricating an exact end time.

Assumptions to flag: the payment provider outage cause is unverified from the provider side (treated as third-party per the service register), no deploy or config change was found in the queried windows, and recovery status is uncertain since metrics ended while the service was still failing.

For the executive summary, I'll avoid naming internal components and just describe customers being unable to load their account page due to an outside payment company's failure. Root cause: a synchronous call to the third-party payment API returning 503 on the card endpoint, with no fallback or timeout isolation, letting the provider's failure cascade into a full account page failure — and I should note the escalation response had limited mitigation options since the dependency sits outside the team's estate.

assumptions: The provider's own failure mode was not observed directly - we only see 503 responses in io-shop's logs, with no data from IO Payments Ltd on what broke on their side or when it would end.

io-pay is treated as third-party and outside the estate Argus may act on, based on the service register; this classification was read, not verified independently, and it is the reason no mitigation was attempted.

'No change caused this' rests on the change and flag lookups that were run (deploys/releases on io-shop and recent flag changes); changes to shared infrastructure, network paths, or credentials outside those queries would not have shown up.

The account page is assumed to depend on the card call on essentially every render, which is why a provider outage translates to near-total page failure; this is inferred from the log pattern and the code path at src/io_shop/payment_provider.py:95, not from a traffic breakdown.
The incident is assumed to have continued past the last minute of metrics read - there is no recovery signal in the data, so end time and total impact are open.
The impact figures quoted in the incident record come from the shop's own traffic measurements; they are reproduced as given and were not recomputed here.
The draft pull request is an untested proposal; it was not reviewed, merged, or deployed during the incident, and it is not established that it would have prevented or shortened this outage.
input.executive_summary: Starting at 22:06 UTC on 28 September 2026, shoppers trying to open their account page on the online shop got errors instead of the page. The cause was outside the shop: an outside payment company's service started rejecting the shop's requests for saved card details, and because the account page waits for that answer before it can be drawn, the failure of the card lookup became a failure of the whole page. Almost all account page traffic was affected for the duration, and the page was still failing at the end of the data reviewed, so the outage lasted at least from 22:06 to that point and the real length and customer cost are not yet known from these records. Automated response detected the problem at 22:11 UTC, confirmed within about a minute that the failing system belongs to the payment company and not to us, and therefore had nothing it was permitted or able to switch, restart, or roll back. It made no changes. Instead it opened a draft code change proposing that the shop stop letting a payment-provider outage take the whole page down, and escalated to humans at 22:18 UTC. Recovery depends on the payment provider; follow-up should cover contacting them and making the account page survive their next outage.
input.root_cause: The third-party payment provider io-pay (api.io-pay.example, IO Payments Ltd) began returning 503s on its card-retrieval endpoint (/v1/shoppers/{id}/card) at 22:06 UTC on 2026-09-28; io-shop's account page calls that endpoint synchronously while rendering (src/io_shop/payment_provider.py:95) with no fallback or degraded path, so every provider failure became a failed page request. No deploy, config, or feature-flag change was found on io-shop in the windows queried, and the rollout was converged on a single revision, which rules out an internal change as the trigger.
